technical-data.invention-title: A METHOD AND SYSTEM ADAPTED TO PERMIT SUBSCRIBERS TO PERSONALISE VALUE ADDED SERVICES
PROCEDE ET SYSTEME PERMETTANT AUX ABONNES DE PERSONNALISER DES SERVICES A VALEUR AJOUTEE

abstract.p: The present invention provides a telecommunications system which can act as a host for value added services. In particular, the present invention provides a mechanism which allows a telecommunications subscriber to personalise such services. The telecommunications system includes a telecommunications operator's server, a plurality of subscriber transceivers, at least one service provider's server, data storage means and a plurality of fixed subscriber data terminals. Each of the plurality of fixed subscriber data terminals is adapted to communicate with the operator's server. At least one service provider's server is adapted to communicate with said operator's server. Each of subscriber transceiver is adapted to communicate with said operator's server. The storage means contains a service data base and is adapted to communicate with said operator's server. The telecommunications system may enable a subscriber to establish a value added service menu facilitating selection of a given value added service from a plurality of value added services. At least some of the subscriber transceivers may be mobile transceivers. The subscriber value added services may be provided by more than one service provider. The operator's server may mediate between a subscriber's transceiver and a service provider's server in the provision of value added services by adapting the value added services in accordance with service settings previously provided by said subscriber from said subscriber's fixed subscriber data terminal.

L'invention concerne un système de télécommunications pouvant servir d'hôte pour des services à valeur ajoutée. L'invention concerne notamment un mécanisme permettant à un abonné à un système de télécommunications de personnaliser lesdits services. Le service de télécommunications comprend un serveur d'opérateur de télécommunications, plusieurs émetteurs-récepteurs d'abonnés, au moins un serveur de fournisseur de services, un moyen de stockage de données et plusieurs terminaux de données d'abonnés fixes. Chaque terminal de données d'abonnés fixes est conçu pour communiquer avec le serveur de l'opérateur. Au moins un serveur de fournisseur de services est conçu pour communiquer avec ledit serveur d'opérateur. Chaque émetteur-récepteur d'abonné est conçu pour communiquer avec ledit serveur d'opérateur. Le moyen de stockage contient une base de données de services et est conçu pour communiquer avec ledit serveur d'opérateur. Le système de télécommunications peut permettre à un abonné d'établir un menu de services à valeur ajoutée, facilitant la sélection d'un service à valeur ajoutée parmi plusieurs services à valeur ajoutée. Au moins certains émetteurs-récepteurs peuvent être mobiles. Les services à valeur ajoutée peuvent être fournis par plus d'un fournisseur de services. Le serveur d'opérateur peut servir d'intermédiaire entre un émetteur-récepteur d'abonné et un serveur de fournisseur de services, pour la fourniture de services à valeur ajoutée, en adaptant les services à valeur ajoutés aux définitions des services produites par ledit abonné depuis ledit terminal de données d'abonné fixe de l'abonné.

description.p: A METHOD AND SYSTEM ADAPTED TO PERMIT SUBSCRIBERS TO PERSONALISE VALUE ADDED SERVICES

The present invention relates to a telecommunications system for providing value added services which subscribers are permitted to personalise, a service platform for use with said telecommunications system, a method of operating said telecommunications system, a subscriber PC for use with said telecommunications system and a mobile transceiver for use with said telecommunications system.

The present invention provides a telecommunications system which can act as a host for value added services. In particular, the present invention provides a mechanism which allows a telecommunications subscriber to personalise such services.

When services are called via a PC, or mobile telephone, it is generally necessary to specify the value of one, or more, input parameters which control the service. Different users often use services in different ways, although it is not unusual for a user to repeatedly enter the same values on different call occasions.

Conventional mobile telephones are not especially suitable for entry of large volumes of text. Thus, when value added services are executed through a mobile telephone transceiver, a user will want to avoid entering characters unnecessarily.
When using a mobile telephone, a user will want to have access to as much specially adapted information and as many specially adapted functions as possible, with a minimum of button pressing.

The present invention can be used as a freestanding technology, but is also included as a component in the telecommunications system described and claimed in our co-pending patent application Kgp 30/99 which relates to a system concept offering a simple methodology of introducing new value added services, subscriber-controlled personalising, and radio resource-saving mobile
services.

Patent application WO98/03005 describes a system which allows a mobile telephone subscriber to re-edit, via a PC, the personal settings of a value added service, such as e-mail. A "formula", indicating the current setting of a value added service is ordered from the service provider's server and is sent to the PC where it can be re-edited. The re-edited "formula" is then returned to the service provider's server where the new settings are stored.
The features of the present invention, set out below, distinguish it from the invention disclosed in WO98/03005.

1. In the invention described in WO98/03005, a "formula" for a given value added service is ordered from a server. Whereas, in the present invention the user receives "pages", which are not entirely analogous to a "formula", that facilitate setting up the service parameters for a value added service. However, there is no one-to-one correspondence between the "pages" and the value added service. The personalisation provided by the present invention is much broader than that described in WO98/03005 and is not fully executed via a simple formula and is mediated by an operator's server. For example, a user may set the parameters relating to a particular service and also choose to create his own menu where different services are included within the same menu. These different services do not even have to be provided by the same service provider.

2. In the invention described in WO98/03005, the "formula", with the current service settings, is downloaded from the service provider's server. In the
present invention the object is not to let the user change the existing settings, but rather to enable the user, himself, to give his own settings, i.e. service parameters. A user can, of course, edit service parameters which he has already entered.

In the invention described in WO98/03005, existing service settings are changed via the service provider's server. In the present invention a server is used, not to change the existing service settings, but rather to give values to the service parameters.

4. In the invention described in WO98/03005, the re-edited formula is returned to the service provider's server and stored to be used as a new "formula". In the present invention, the settings for the traditional operator's network elements are not changed by the subscriber. Rather, the subscriber is enabled to adapt a service to his own needs. These value added services are not connected to the traditional network elements but are executed by service providers on their own servers. Such service providers may be entirely independent of the telecommunications operator via whom the services are offered to the subscriber. Furthermore, subscriber modified service parameters are stored by the operator on a special database which is not related to any network element. This means that no changes are executed on any network element, as is the case with the invention described in WO98/03005. Again, the present invention is based on the subscriber settings being used to call a service via a special operator's server, rather than being loaded on to a service provider's server. The operator's server calls a requested service and adapts the service from settings previously given by the subscriber.

5. In the invention described in WO98/03005, a receipt is given for a re- edited formula. In the present invention, the user can interactively personalise a service which provides a user interface via which service parameters are entered. It is, of course, possible for a subscriber to obtain some form of receipt for the parameters he has stored in the database of personalised services, but it is probably easier for a subscriber to select a
service and obtain information regarding the parameter entries he has previously made.
Embodiments of the invention will now be described, by way of example, with reference to the accompanying drawing, in which:
Figure 1 illustrates a schematic view of a telecommunications system according to the present invention.

The present invention is based on a mobile telephone user being able to adapt value added services to his personal needs. For this to be possible, the services must be parameter-controlled, which implies that the behaviour of a service can be controlled with the aid of the value of one, or more, parameters added when the service is called.

To facilitate the description of the invention, reference should initially be made to Fig. 1 , where a simplified version of a system according to the present invention is shown. Two users, "X" and "Y", choose to personalise service "A" offered via an operator. Service "A" is available on a service provider's server and must be called with three input parameters. Service "B" is also included to illustrate how menu-based services can be called.
The present invention can, of course, operate with many subscribers and can handle many more than two service providers, each of which may supply one, or more, value added services.

To ensure that personalisation is as user-friendly as possible, this can be performed, e.g. through a user being able to surf into a specific home page, (www....). The Web page gives access to a web-based user interface in the operator's server. With the aid of this web page it is possible to see which services are available and also to have access to a user interface to personalise these services.

The procedure to be used, by a subscriber, to personalise a service will
described.

1. The subscriber selects service "A", say, via a web interface and receives information, via the operator's server, that the service requires 3 parameters for a call. Details of all available services that can be accessed through the operator can be stored in a service database.

2. The subscriber chooses to enter values for parameter 1 and parameter 2. It should be noted that a user has both the opportunity to specify different values for a parameter and the opportunity to refrain from specifying a value. The different values allowed can be defined in a user interface, e.g. the numerals 1- 100, or on/off. By refraining from predefining the value for parameter 3, the user is deferring the setting of this parameter to the time of service execution. An alternative approach to personalising a service is for the user to specify default values for all parameters when personalising the service and then, if necessary, overriding the default values at the time of service execution.
3. When the user is ready, he can specify a name for the personalised service. This name is used if the user wishes to call the service directly via the keypad on a mobile telephone.

4. The operator's server can also create a unique identity for the personalised service. This identity is used when a service is called via a menu selection. A personalised service must be identifiable either via a unique identity, or via a unique name. However, it is also conceivable to use a combination of name and A-number, or identity and A-number, to identify a personalised service.

5. The result is saved in a database, the personalised service database, where each subscriber can save data relating to his own
personalised services. The database is linked to the operator's server, which implies that the settings are valid until the subscriber accesses and changes them on a subsequent occasion.
6. A subscriber can, in a similar way, personalise a number of services.

7. If a subscriber wishes to have access to different personalised services via a menu structure, he can create a menu structure with the aid of a tool offered via the operator's server and moreover link the personalised services to different menu choices in this menu structure, e.g. a menu choice calls a personalised version of service "A", and a number of menu choices call a personalised version of service "B".
8. The user interface, in the form of a menu, can then be sent to the mobile telephone.
The way in which a subscriber, subscriber "X", uses a personalised service will now be described.
1. The subscriber selects a service via a menu choice, for example service "A".

2. Included in the user interface that has been downloaded is information on the number of parameters for which the user must enter values. This means that the subscriber will be prompted to enter values for these parameters. In the example described here, where subscriber "X" has personalised service "A" by entering predefined values for parameters 1 and 2 in the operator's server, the mobile telephone will now prompt the subscriber to enter values for the other parameters, i.e. parameter 3. The principle employed is that the parameters which have not been assigned predefined values in the operator's server must have values assigned by the
mobile telephone.

3. When the subscriber has selected a service and entered values for any possible parameters, a message is sent to the operator's server. This message contains the unique identity of the service, or an unambiguous reference to the identity, and the value of the entered parameters.

4. When the operator's server receives this message, the unique identity, or the unique reference to the identity, is used as a search word in the database. The database returns the service to be called and also the predefined parameter values stored when the subscriber personalised the service.

5. The operator's server now creates a message, a service call for service "A", where all parameters are included, i.e. parameters 1 and 2 from the operator's server and parameter 3 from the mobile telephone.
6. Service "A" is called with the parameters which user "X" has specified both via the Internet, when personalising the service, and via the mobile telephone, when executing the service.

If subscriber "Y" chooses to enter values for all input parameters for service "A" when personalising the service, this means that no parameters need be specified on service execution, which, in turn, means that "Y" can use an advanced service called from a conventional mobile telephone in an extremely simple manner.
It should be noted that it is possible for a subscriber to call several different types of personalised services via a menu structure.

It is also possible for a user to personalise a specific service in several different ways. This means that a service can be called either without any values
for the input parameters needing to be specified from the mobile telephone keypad, which makes the service very easy to use, or, alternatively, that it is possible to specify values of input parameters using the keypad of a mobile telephone, or transceiver, i.e. the service can be controlled from the mobile telephone on service execution.

If a subscriber has, when personalising a service, specified a name for the personalised service, this service can be called without a menu structure being downloaded to the mobile telephone. This can then take place through the subscriber making a call for the service via, for example, a conventional SMS.

This can take place through the name and different parameters being separated by predefined characters. An example of such a message might be: (Unf*1400*Vargen), which may result in all members of the Unf group receiving an SMS with the text: "Unf meeting at Vargen at 14.00". Note that the issued text is more extensive than that entered. The amount of information that can be added depends entirely on how the service is arranged, additional information can be entered as parameters when the service is personalised.

The description of the present invention, presented above, assumes that a service is personalised via an Internet-connected PC, which is likely to be the most attractive method. Updating of the operator's server database with personalisation data can, naturally, be performed with the aid of any computer whatever connected to the operator's server via a fixed connection, or via a radio connection. Personalisation of a service may also conceivably be performed from a mobile telephone via a specially adapted function in the mobile telephone which communicates with a corresponding function in the operator's server.

A subscriber may also conceivably be given the opportunity to enter default values for parameters when personalising a service. This would mean that these parameter values are valid if a customer has not chosen to specify values for these parameters via the mobile telephone keypad. Information on a parameter having been assigned a default value may be downloaded to the mobile telephone, but this is not necessary, since a user can, for example, when personalising a service make a paper printout of the default values valid for that
service.

The present invention provides a general technology which can be used where there is a need to save bandwidth and offers subscribers an opportunity, on the basis of general services, to create their own personalised services. The technology is independent of the mobile telephony system (GSM, UMTS, etc.) and the carrier service, as well as terminal technology. The technology is especially suited to offering personalised services to mobile telephones with a conventional keypad by giving subscribers an opportunity to enter parameter values, prior to using the service, via a PC coupled to the Internet, which means that these parameters need not be given any value when a service is called from a mobile telephone. A personalised service can be called with a minimum of buttons having to be pressed.
The present invention enables:
mobile services to be personalised by subscribers themselves via e.g. an Internet-connected PC;

- subscribers to choose, prior to using a service, to enter values for a number of parameters needed when a service is called and in this way avoid the need to enter values for these parameters via the mobile telephone keypad when executing a service;
- subscribers to specify their own names for services and, in this way, more easily memorise how different services are to be called; and

subscribers to create their own menus which can be downloaded to mobile telephones supporting the use of menus - by enabling personalised services to be called via a personalised menu, user- friendliness is substantially increased.
